Physical exercise strongly affects human metabolism and causes biochemical changes. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between routine plasma biomarker levels and recovery efficiency in soccer players during an entire competitive match season. The players participating in the study were divided into a midfielder/defender group (seven midfielders and seven defenders) and a goalie/substitute group (six persons—goalkeepers and players with a short cumulative match-time). The fasting capillary blood samples were taken 17–24 h after each competitive match. The blood plasma was used to determine the creatinine, urea, alkaline phosphatase, creatine kinase, lactate dehydrogenase, aspartate and alanine aminotransferase, iron and magnesium levels of the athletes. The levels of (AST) (aspartate aminotransferase), (ALT) (alanine aminotransferase) and (Cr) creatinine were higher in the midfielder/defender group than in the control group, but only AST and Cr significantly varied over time (AST decreased, and Cr increased with time). The (LDH) (lactate dehydrogenase) activity and urea level were significantly lower in the midfielder/defender group than in the goalie/substitute group, and it significantly varied over time (LDH decreased, and urea increased with time). No differences in the (CK) creatine kinase and (ALP) alkaline phosphatase activities between the groups was found, although CK increased significantly with time in the midfielder/defender group (particularly midfielders in the spring round). In midfielders, the AST activity and the iron level were significantly lower in the spring than in the autumn round. On the contrary, ALT, CK, urea and magnesium levels were significantly higher in the spring than in autumn round. A long-term measurement of biochemical parameters in elite soccer players indicated that AST, CK, LDH and creatinine levels, when analyzed together, could constitute a useful set of markers for monitoring recovery periods. exercise physical fitness recovery biochemical markers 1. Introduction Physical exercise strongly affects human metabolism and causes biochemical changes. This is reflected in the results of laboratory analyses of changes in serum parameters, which indicate degrees of fatigue. It is extremely important to provide sport physicians, coaches and all persons involved in sport more comprehensive information about the response of organisms to ordered training [ 1 ]. The many faces of different types of training and the variety of physiological reactions of trainees explain why sport medicine is still looking for a perfect way to monitor the effects of training. There is an enormous need for markers that describe an organisms’ answers to physical exercise. Current knowledge on clinical chemistry is still expanding and growing. There is a continuing search for new markers and parameters that could be useful for daily use. The monitoring of athletes’ training should be performed using measurements of their performance and biological or physiological parameters. Muscle metabolism parameters, like creatine kinase (CK), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and myoglobin, are usually increased after exercise [ 2 ]. An increase in these variables may represent an index of cellular necrosis and tissue damage, following acute and chronic muscle injuries [ 3 , 4 ]. Noakes reported that the increase in CK, after long-duration exercise, is more closely related to the duration of exercise than its intensity [ 5 ]. Professional soccer players participating in daily training have consistently high resting CK values [ 6 ]. The post-exercise growth pattern in CK activity is very specific. CK usually increases after 24–36 h of strenuous exercise, which makes this biomarker a valuable tool for monitoring recovery efficiency. Similarly, LDH, as a muscle damage marker, should be verified [ 3 , 7 ]. Serum creatinine concentration is a known parameter for measuring renal function in clinical medicine. In sports medicine, creatinine is useful as an indicator of the general health status and water-electrolyte balance in a patient. However, it is important to note that serum creatinine concentration is higher in athletes than in the population of people who are not physically active [ 8 ]. There is also a strong correlation between the BMI (Body Mass Index) unit, sport performed and creatinine concentration, because there were different kinds of training and involvement of aerobic and anaerobic metabolism [ 7 ]. These changes suggest that monitoring the plasma creatinine level should be verified as a recovery efficiency biomarker. While urea is not specific enough to monitor renal function, monitoring urea concentration in professional athletes can provide some important information. The normalization of the serum urea level might be a signal that a strenuous training session has begun, when this parameter is regularly monitored [ 9 , 10 , 11 ]. For that reason, the plasma urea level should be considered as a recovery parameter, like creatinine. Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) serve as markers of liver disease, and increases in AST, ALT, and LDH have been observed, after an endurance effort, such as an ultramarathon [ 12 , 13 , 14 ]. It was also found that AST, ALT, and γ-glutamyltransferase (GGT) activities could be valuable tools for assessing people’s metabolic response to exercise. Soccer training and matches also induce alkaline phosphatase (ALP), which leaks from the skeletal muscles. ALP is involved in ATP metabolism during exercise by the participation in amino acid catabolism and the hydrolysis of fats across cell membranes [ 15 ]. Therefore, monitoring those well-known diagnostic markers, such as enzymes, as mentioned above, could prevent athletes from overreaching or overtraining [ 16 ]. Thus, they also could be suitable for recovery efficiency monitoring. An insufficient recovery time during the soccer match season may lead to fatigue and may predispose players to mineral deficiency. One of the most important micronutrients is iron (Fe), and an iron deficiency may be linked with the development of anemia and the impairment of athletic performance [ 17 , 18 ]. Another relevant micronutrient is magnesium (Mg), which is the cofactor of over 325 enzymatic reactions linked with anaerobic performance, including muscle contraction and relaxation. Mg takes part in regulating troponin expression via calcium ion concentration gradients, which may have an impact on enhancing muscle strength [ 19 , 20 ]. For that reason, measuring plasma iron and magnesium levels in soccer players might be an additional tool for monitoring recovery efficiency. An ideal biochemical indicator for assessing the degree of body recovery would be a marker that responds only to physical exercise and reacts in a predictable and permanent manner. Every sport has its own specificity. A previous study indicates that elite soccer players are characterized by significant changes in biochemical and hematological parameters over a half-season, which are linked to the training workload, as well as the adaptation induced by the soccer training [ 21 ]. No study has yet followed the same team of highly trained professional soccer players repeatedly over a whole season. The present work described the results of a long-term study, performed on elite soccer players of the soccer club, Pogoń S.A. The research was carried out during the whole year of premier league games, both in the spring and autumn rounds. The aim of the study was to investigate the relationship between routine plasma biomarker levels and recovery efficiency in soccer players during an entire competitive match season.

extracted_data.document_summary: This study investigated the relationship between routine plasma biomarker levels and recovery efficiency in elite professional soccer players over an entire eleven-month competitive match season, including seasonal variations and differences based on player position and cumulative match time. It concluded that a panel of AST, CK, LDH, and creatinine can effectively monitor recovery, adaptation, and overtraining risk, particularly in active positions like midfielders who may also be prone to iron and magnesium deficiencies.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Competitive professional soccer matches and regular intense training
treatment_details.dose_specificity: An eleven-month competitive season, comprising 44 league and cup matches (23 autumn, 21 spring), typically one to two matches per week. Fasting capillary blood samples were collected 17-24 hours after each match. The study compared player positions (midfielder/defender vs. goalie/substitute, and individual midfielder/defender subgroups), noting significant differences in cumulative match time and physical demands. No explicit dose-response comparisons were reported for training intensity, but adaptation to increasing training load was observed.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: higher, increased over time, and varied by group/season
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Generally higher in midfielder/defender groups compared to goalie/substitute groups, particularly in midfielders, with concentration increasing significantly over time during the season (e.g., in midfielder/defender group, goalie/substitute autumn round, midfielders spring round). It showed a slight but significant positive correlation with cumulative match-time in midfielder/defender groups (R=0.24-0.25, P<=0.05) and goalies/substitutes (R=0.26, P<=0.05), and a stronger positive correlation in midfielders (R=0.17-0.41, P<=0.05). However, a negative correlation was observed in defenders (R=-0.28, P<=0.05) with cumulative game time.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Waste product of muscle metabolism and creatine breakdown, indicating muscle mass, kidney function, and general health status. It is involved in water-electrolyte balance.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Throughout an eleven-month professional competitive soccer match season, including post-match recovery (17-24 hours post-match), regular intense training, and competition. Comparisons were made between midfielder/defender and goalie/substitute groups, and individual midfielder/defender subgroups, considering cumulative game time and seasonal variations (autumn vs. spring rounds).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: A useful biomarker for monitoring recovery periods and efficiency, reflecting muscle mass, creatine turnover, and kidney stress from intense physical activity. It indicates dynamic changes in muscle metabolism and hydration status over the season, suggesting adaptation or increased demands depending on player position and game time. Its lower interindividual variability makes it a good indicator for assessing recovery, adaptation, and reducing overtraining risk.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: varied by group/season; lower, increased over time, and higher in spring vs. autumn
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Levels were generally lower in the midfielder/defender group compared to the goalie/substitute group, but surprisingly highest in the goalie/substitute group. It increased significantly over time in the midfielder/defender group (especially in spring, R=0.16, P<=0.05) and in midfielders during the spring round compared to autumn. A decreasing trend over time was noticed in these groups (significant negative correlation with match-time for the season, e.g., in goalie/substitute group: R=-0.20 to -0.33, P<=0.05).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Waste product of protein metabolism, indicating protein catabolism, hydration status, and kidney function. Its levels are influenced by amino acid metabolism and cortisol.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Throughout an eleven-month professional competitive soccer match season, including post-match recovery, regular intense training, and competition. Comparisons were made between midfielder/defender and goalie/substitute groups, and individual midfielder/defender subgroups, considering cumulative game time and seasonal variations (autumn vs. spring rounds).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Considered a recovery parameter, its normalization may signal readiness for strenuous training. Levels indicate protein catabolism, hydration status, and metabolic stress, with higher levels in less active players potentially implying less efficient adaptation or increased training load. It can reflect adaptation to training but its utility as a sole indicator for body fatigue and recovery is debated.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: varied over time (increase in autumn, decrease in spring)
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant differences were found between midfielder/defender and goalie/substitute groups. However, activity varied significantly over time: generally increasing in the autumn round (R=0.18-0.29, P<=0.05 for various groups) and subsequently decreasing in the spring round (R=-0.25 to -0.60, P<=0.05 for various groups).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Enzyme involved in ATP metabolism, amino acid catabolism, and hydrolysis of fats across cell membranes, potentially leaking from skeletal muscles. It also indicates bone metabolism, liver function, and various other metabolic processes.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Throughout an eleven-month professional competitive soccer match season, including post-match recovery and regular intense training. Changes were observed across autumn and spring rounds, and were correlated with cumulative game time in midfielder/defender, goalie/substitute, midfielder, and defender groups.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Suitable for recovery efficiency monitoring, its changes over time may indicate adaptation to training load. It can also reflect dynamic changes in bone turnover or liver function across competitive phases, and post-effort activity could signal early symptoms of vitamin B6 and niacin deficiency. Monitoring could help prevent overreaching or overtraining.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: increased significantly over time, higher in spring vs. autumn, decreased in goalie/substitutes
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: While no significant differences were found between player groups, CK activity generally increased significantly over time, especially in the spring round for midfielder/defender groups and midfielders. It showed a slight but significant positive correlation with cumulative match-time in midfielder/defender groups (R=0.14-0.17, P<=0.05) and for midfielders (R=0.30, P<=0.05) and defenders (R=0.23, P<=0.05) over the entire season. In contrast, it decreased with time in the goalie/substitute group (R=-0.22 to -0.23, P<=0.05). It is generally expected to be permanently elevated in professional soccer players and usually increases after 24-36 hours of strenuous exercise.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: An enzyme involved in energy metabolism and production in muscle cells, serving as a primary marker of muscle damage, cellular necrosis, and tissue integrity following acute and chronic muscle injuries. It also indicates metabolic stress.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Throughout an eleven-month professional competitive soccer match season, encompassing daily training, strenuous exercise, and post-match recovery (17-24 hours post-match). Observations were made across different player positions (midfielder/defender, goalie/substitute, individual midfielder and defender subgroups), considering cumulative game time and seasonal variations (autumn vs. spring rounds).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: A valuable and useful marker for monitoring recovery periods, reflecting muscle damage levels, cumulative muscle damage, and physiological stress from intense muscular effort. However, due to its large interindividual variability and constant elevation in professional soccer players, it might be unsuitable as a sole parameter for monitoring the recovery process. It contributes to assessing recovery efficiency, adaptation, and diminishing the risk of overreaching or injury.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: lower in midfielder/defender, decreased over time, but generally increases after exercise
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Activity was surprisingly highest in the goalie/substitute group compared to midfielder/defender groups. It generally showed a decreasing trend over time in various groups and phases (e.g., midfielder/defender group decreased significantly over time, R=-0.29, P<=0.05 in spring; goalie/substitute group decreased, R=-0.22 to -0.31, P<=0.05 over season). However, it is generally known to increase after exercise and endurance efforts, but for defenders, it showed a decrease in spring (R=-0.29, P<=0.05) but an increase over the total season (R=-0.23, P<=0.05).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: An enzyme involved in energy metabolism (glycolysis) that catalyzes the conversion between pyruvate and lactate. It serves as an indicator of anaerobic metabolism, cellular damage, tissue necrosis, and metabolic stress.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Throughout an eleven-month professional competitive soccer match season, including post-match recovery (17-24 hours post-match), regular intense training, and after exercise/endurance efforts. Comparisons were made between midfielder/defender and goalie/substitute groups, and individual midfielder/defender subgroups, considering cumulative game time and seasonal variations (autumn vs. spring rounds).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: A useful muscle damage marker for monitoring recovery periods and efficiency, indicating cellular necrosis, tissue damage, and metabolic stress. Lower levels in active players might suggest better adaptation or less damage, while higher levels in less active players could imply poorer adaptation. Its activity might also depend on diet, potentially making it less effective as a recovery marker. Its lower interindividual variability is beneficial for assessing recovery, adaptation, and reducing overtraining risk.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: higher initially, then consistently decreased over time, lower in spring vs. autumn
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Generally higher in midfielder/defender groups, especially midfielders, compared to goalie/substitute groups. AST levels consistently decreased significantly over time and with cumulative game time across all player subgroups and seasonal rounds (negative correlation ranging from R=-0.32 to -0.50, P<=0.05). Activity was significantly lower in the spring round compared to the autumn round across all positions. While generally increasing after an endurance effort, the long-term trend in this study was a decrease.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: An enzyme involved in amino acid metabolism (catalyzes transamination) and is stimulated by cortisol. It serves as an indicator of liver disease, muscle damage, metabolic stress, and recovery processes, reflecting both liver and muscle integrity.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Throughout an eleven-month professional competitive soccer match season, including post-match recovery (17-24 hours post-match), regular intense training, and after endurance efforts. Comparisons were made between different player positions (midfielder/defender, goalie/substitute, individual midfielder and defender subgroups), considering cumulative game time, seasonal variations (autumn vs. spring rounds), and adaptation to training.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: An appropriate and useful biomarker for monitoring recovery efficiency, metabolic response to exercise, and adaptation to training, as it is less affected by other factors and has lower interindividual variability than CK. It indicates physiological stress and muscle damage levels, suggesting higher strain in active positions, and its decrease over time often suggests adaptation or reduced tissue stress/damage. Monitoring AST can help prevent overreaching or overtraining and can appear earlier than CK in assessing recovery.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: higher in midfielder/defender groups, higher in spring for midfielders, lower in spring for defenders and goalie/substitutes, and increases after endurance effort
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Levels were generally higher in midfielder/defender groups, particularly in midfielders, compared to goalie/substitute groups. Midfielders showed significantly higher ALT activity in the spring round compared to autumn, while defenders showed lower activity in spring compared to autumn. It also increased after an endurance effort. However, ALT decreased significantly over time with cumulative game time in the goalie/substitute group (R=-0.33 to -0.40, P<=0.05) and showed a slight negative correlation in midfielders during the autumn round (R=-0.25, P<=0.05).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: An enzyme involved in amino acid metabolism (catalyzes transamination) and is stimulated by cortisol. It serves as a marker of liver disease, muscle damage, liver function, and general cellular damage, reflecting metabolic response to exercise.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Throughout an eleven-month professional competitive soccer match season, including post-match recovery (17-24 hours post-match), regular intense training, and after endurance efforts. Comparisons were made between different player positions (midfielder/defender, goalie/substitute, individual midfielder and defender subgroups), considering cumulative game time, seasonal variations (autumn vs. spring rounds), and adaptation to training.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Valuable for assessing recovery efficiency, its annual changes primarily reflect adaptation to increases in training load. It indicates physiological stress, muscle damage, and liver stress, suggesting higher strain in more active player positions. Monitoring ALT can help prevent athletes from overreaching or overtraining.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: lower in midfielder/defender groups, decreasing trend over season, varied by season/group
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Generally lower in the midfielder/defender group compared to the goalie/substitute group, especially in the spring round for midfielders compared to autumn. A decreasing trend was observed over the season, with significant decreases in midfielders over the entire season (R=-0.33, P<=0.05) and for the midfielder/defender group (R=-0.15, P<=0.05). However, it also increased significantly with time in the spring round for the midfielder/defender group, and showed a positive correlation with cumulative game time for defenders (R=0.23, P<=0.05).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: An essential micronutrient vital for oxygen transport (hemoglobin), energy metabolism, and various cellular processes. Its levels reflect the body's physiological stress response, and its deficiency is linked with anemia.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Throughout an eleven-month professional competitive soccer match season, including post-match recovery, regular intense training, and conditions of insufficient recovery time and mineral deficiency. Comparisons were made between different player positions (midfielder/defender, goalie/substitute, individual midfielder and defender subgroups), considering cumulative game time, seasonal variations (autumn vs. spring rounds), and the prolonged intensive physical activity of active players like midfielders.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Deficiency can impair athletic performance, and its measurement can be an additional tool for monitoring recovery efficiency. Levels indicate physiological stress, increased iron utilization/loss, altered iron metabolism, or inflammation due to intense exercise. It suggests dynamic changes in iron status, reflecting recovery, dietary intake, or red blood cell turnover. Midfielders, experiencing prolonged intensive activity, are more prone to deficiencies, warranting screening for health reasons.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: generally lower with cumulative time, higher in spring vs. autumn for midfielders, and increased in spring for midfielders
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant differences in baseline levels were found between player subgroups. However, magnesium levels generally decreased significantly over time and showed a negative correlation with cumulative match time in the midfielder/defender group (R=-0.16 to -0.30, P<=0.05 for various phases), midfielders (R=-0.19 to -0.30, P<=0.05), and defenders (R=-0.32, P<=0.05). Conversely, midfielders exhibited significantly higher plasma magnesium levels in the spring round compared to the autumn round, and also increased significantly with time in spring.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: An essential mineral and cofactor for over 325 enzymatic reactions, crucial for anaerobic performance, muscle contraction and relaxation, nerve function, blood glucose control, and energy production. It is involved in regulating troponin expression via calcium ion gradients and plays a role in glucose availability and lactate clearance in muscles during exercise.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Throughout an eleven-month professional competitive soccer match season, including post-match recovery, conditions of insufficient recovery time, and mineral deficiency. Observations were made across various player positions (midfielder/defender, individual midfielder and defender subgroups), considering cumulative game time and seasonal variations (autumn vs. spring rounds).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Measurement can be an additional tool for monitoring recovery efficiency, as it reflects electrolyte balance, physiological stress, and potential depletion or increased utilization due to intense activity. It may suggest altered mineral balance, cellular shifts, or the need for supplementation, especially for active players like midfielders who are prone to deficiencies, particularly in the spring season. It can impact enhancing muscle strength and indicates progressive electrolyte depletion with increased playing time.
